To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
male ornamentation and within pair paternity were not associated with the rate of food-provisioning to nestlings in the scarlet rosethinch Carpodacus erthrinus.

(i) male provisioning rates in rosefinches do not depend on their paternity in their nest, (ii) male provisioning rates do not depend on male ornamentation and (iii) the ability to sire extrapair offspring is associated with higher provisioning rates.

in a socially monogamous passerine species with high levels of extra-pair fertilization, male ornamentation is not associated with parental care intensity, and that males that lose paternities do not reduce their provisioning rates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of the ‘good parent’ model in relation to male ornamentation and the occurrence of extra pair offspring in a socially monogamous species, the scarlet rose finch.
the relationship between male ornamentation, male parental care, male paternity and extra-pair paternities.
a possible trade-off between the direct and indirect benefits of extra-pair mating in a socially monogamous bird.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the good parent model is rejected in scarlet rose-finches, whereas parental investment theory seems to apply to this population.
male parental care is not associated with male ornamentation and paternity in scarlet rose-finches, but male ornamentation is associated with male extra-pair mating success.
male ornamentation in rosefinches does not signal direct benefits to females and is unlikely to have been selected as a signal of direct benefits.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in this species, the ‘good parent’ model is not supported by the data, whereas the ‘parental investment’ model is supported.
male ornamentation and within- pair paternity are not related to male provisioning rates in the scarlet finch.
the occurrence of extra pair paternity in the scarlet finch is not associated with a decrease in the male parental care intensity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evolution of male ornamentation is not associated with male parental care in scarlet rose finches.
the occurrence of extra pair paternity and the intensity of male parental care are not necessarily linked in the scarlet finches.
, at least in this species, male parental effort does not depend on the occurrence of extra pair offspring in the nest, nor on the male's ability to sire them.
